title: Pascal's Triangle II

blocks.text: Given a number rowIndex (starting from 0), return only that one row of Pascal's triangle, using no more than O(rowIndex) extra memory beyond the row itself.

blocks.title: Analogy: Asking for Only One Level of the Bean Machine
blocks.text: Picture the same bean machine from before, where each level counts the number of paths to every position. This time, someone only wants to know the counts for one specific level, say level 4, and has no interest in seeing every level that came before it. Building and keeping every earlier level just to answer about level 4 is more work and more shelf space than the question actually calls for.

blocks.caption: Only the target row needs to exist in memory at the end

blocks.text: The row at index 1 is simply [1, 1], the second row of the triangle.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what the explicit space limit is actually telling us.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The problem only asks for one specific row, not the whole triangle, and explicitly limits extra space to O(rowIndex), a strong hint that keeping every earlier row around is the wrong shape of solution.

Observation 2: Building the target row still requires the values from the row directly above it, but once a row has been used to build the next one, that used-up row is never needed again.

Observation 3: If only one row's worth of memory is reused instead of allocating a brand new row every time, the space requirement can be met exactly, as long as updates are done carefully so a value is not overwritten before something else still needs to read it.

Observation 4: Taking this even further, the multiplicative single-row relationship used to build a row from its own earlier values means the target row's values can be computed directly, without ever building any of the earlier rows at all.
That reasoning alone already sketches the full path: reuse one array carefully, then realize even that single array's history is not strictly required.

The most direct approach is to build the entire triangle from row 0 up to rowIndex, exactly as in the full triangle problem, and then return only the final row, discarding everything else that was built along the way.

items: Start with row 0, which is just [1].
Build each following row from the previous one, summing adjacent values.
Keep every row built so far, even though only the last one will actually be returned.
Once row rowIndex has been built, return it.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: build every row, but only the last one is ever used

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every previously built row is kept inside triangle, even though only the very last one will ever be returned, deliberately mirroring the full Pascal's Triangle solution to make the wasted memory obvious.

The row-building logic itself, 1s at the edges, sum of the two above for interior positions, is identical to the full triangle problem, since a single row of Pascal's triangle is built by exactly the same rule as any other row.
The target row is indexed out at the very end, discarding every other row implicitly, which is exactly the wasted work the next sections remove.

blocks.text: This works because it directly builds the triangle level by level, and the requested row is guaranteed to be present once the loop finishes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rowIndex squared), since building each of the rowIndex rows costs work proportional to its own length.
Space: O(rowIndex squared), since every earlier row is kept in memory alongside the final one, even though the problem only asks for O(rowIndex) space.

Limitation: only the most recently built row is ever needed to build the next one. Every row before that is dead weight, taking up memory that the problem's own space requirement says should not be used.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why keeping every row works but wastes memory: the problem explicitly only wants O(rowIndex) space, and storing rowIndex separate rows uses far more than that.

What is actually needed at each step: only the most recently built row, since that is the only one the next row's values depend on.

Can one single array be reused across every row instead of allocating a new one each time: yes, as long as updates happen in an order that never reads an already-overwritten value.

Which direction avoids that problem: updating right to left, since position j's new value depends on the old value at position j minus 1, which has not been touched yet if positions are updated from the right end inward.

The core idea: reuse a single growing array, updated in place from right to left.

Instead of storing every row, reuse a single array and update it in place as each new row is built. The trick is updating positions from right to left: since position j's new value depends on the old value at position j minus 1, updating right to left means that old value has not been overwritten yet when it is needed.
This keeps only one row worth of memory alive at any time, exactly matching the O(rowIndex) space requirement.

Start with a single row containing just [1]. For each new row, append a trailing 1, then walk backward from the second-to-last position to position 1, updating each value in place by adding the value to its left.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one array, updated right to left, reused across every row

blocks.text: This works because updating from right to left guarantees that whenever position j is about to be updated, to become the sum of the old position j and the old position j minus 1, position j minus 1 has not been touched yet during this pass, so its value is still the correct one from the previous row. Updating left to right instead would overwrite position j minus 1 before position j gets a chance to read its original value, silently corrupting the result.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Update direction is right to left","Every position reads its left neighbor's untouched, previous-row value before that neighbor is itself updated","Correct row values, identical to building a fresh row each time"],["Update direction is left to right (incorrect)","A position's left neighbor gets overwritten with its new value before the current position reads it","Wrong values, since the current position ends up summing two already-updated numbers instead of the original row above"]]}

items: row.append(1) extends the array by exactly one position before the inner update loop runs, since every new row is exactly one element longer than the row before it.
The inner loop runs from i minus 1 down to just above 0, specifically skipping position 0, since the very first position in every row is always 1 and never needs updating.
Each update reads the value just to its left before that neighboring position can possibly be overwritten in this same pass, precisely because the loop counts downward.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rowIndex squared), still building every intermediate row along the way.
Space: O(rowIndex), a genuine improvement, only a single array is ever alive, exactly meeting the problem's space requirement.
10. Further Optimization: Skip the Intermediate Rows Entirely

The optimized solution still does O(rowIndex squared) work, because it builds every row from 0 up to rowIndex along the way, even though none of those intermediate rows are ever returned. The multiplicative binomial coefficient relationship makes it possible to compute the target row's values directly, one position at a time, with no intermediate rows built at all.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: compute the target row directly, no other rows ever built

items: Unlike the in-place update version, this loop never references any previous row at all, not even implicitly, every new value is derived purely from the immediately preceding value within the same target row.

The formula value times (rowIndex minus col plus 1) divided by col is the same multiplicative binomial coefficient relationship used to build a single row directly in the full Pascal's Triangle problem, applied here as the entire solution rather than as a further refinement on top of a row-by-row build.
Because no row before rowIndex is ever constructed, not even temporarily, this is the only version whose time complexity actually matches its space complexity, both O(rowIndex).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rowIndex), a genuine complexity class improvement, since only the target row's own positions are ever touched, no earlier rows are built at all.
Space: O(rowIndex), matching the required output size exactly, with no auxiliary structure beyond it.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is recognizing that needing only one result, instead of every intermediate result along the way, often opens the door to a direct formula that skips the intermediate work entirely. Going from "build everything, keep everything" to "build everything, keep only the latest" to "compute only the answer directly" is a natural progression worth applying whenever a problem asks for just one output out of a whole sequence.

items: Updating the in-place row from left to right instead of right to left, which overwrites values before they are used and produces wrong answers.
Forgetting that rowIndex is 0-indexed, so rowIndex = 0 should return just [1].
Recomputing the entire triangle when the problem specifically only wants one row, missing the O(rowIndex) space requirement.

blocks.text: This problem is a natural follow up to the full Pascal's Triangle problem, and interviewers often use it specifically to test whether a candidate notices the tighter space requirement and adapts accordingly. Proposing the right-to-left in-place update, and then the direct multiplicative formula, shows a clear progression of tightening both space and time.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this in O(rowIndex) space", think: reuse one array, updated right to left, instead of storing every row.
If the interviewer says "why right to left specifically", think: it is the only update order that never reads an already-overwritten value.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid building any earlier rows at all", think: the direct multiplicative formula computes the target row's values with no other row ever built.

items: Why does updating left to right silently produce wrong answers, while right to left does not?

The full Pascal's Triangle problem, whose row-above recurrence and multiplicative single-row shortcut are both reused here, just applied to a single target row instead of every row.
Any 1D dynamic programming problem where a 2D table can be collapsed down to a single reused array, provided updates happen in the correct direction relative to their dependencies.
The 0/1 knapsack style right-to-left update trick, which uses the exact same reasoning: updating in an order that avoids reading an already-overwritten value in the same pass.
"Only the final result matters" problems in general, where skipping every intermediate state, not just compressing it, is possible once the direct relationship between input and output is understood.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach uses O(rowIndex squared) time and space. The in-place right-to-left update brings space down to O(rowIndex) while keeping O(rowIndex squared) time. The multiplicative formula reaches the strongest result, O(rowIndex) time and O(rowIndex) space, a genuine complexity class improvement on both fronts by never building any row except the one actually requested.

items: Pattern: needing only one result out of a whole sequence of intermediate results, which unlocks first a memory optimization, reuse one array, then a full skip of the intermediate work, a direct formula.

Core Idea: a single array can be reused across every row if updates happen right to left, so an old value is never read after being overwritten; going further, the multiplicative row relationship lets the target row be computed directly with no other row ever built.
Time: O(rowIndex squared) for the brute force and optimized versions, O(rowIndex) for the further optimized direct formula.
Space: O(rowIndex squared) for the brute force, O(rowIndex) for both optimized versions.

Most Important Observation: this problem's real constraint is the explicit O(rowIndex) space requirement, which rules out the brute force outright regardless of how correct it is, and rewards recognizing that only one row's memory, or none at all, is ever truly needed.
Interview Difficulty: easy to get a correct but space-violating answer; meeting the actual stated space requirement, and then removing intermediate rows entirely, is what separates the answers.
One line memory trick: update right to left to reuse one array, or skip rows entirely with the multiplicative formula.
